content: I have just opened #42947. Hopefully the statement of the theorem is uncontroversial but I would like feedback on the method of proof and whether any of those lemmas should be made public and/or generalised

Thanks for the PR! The statement is controversial, though :-). It would be better to state it for a compact invariant set (instead of a compact space), assuming only that the function is continuous on this set. Because many proofs use this stronger version.

I have also thought about this but I was not able to have time to implement this, and I claim that we can prove the following more general version:

import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Integral.RieszMarkovKakutani.Real

open MeasureTheory

variable {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [LocallyCompactSpace X]
  [MeasurableSpace X] [BorelSpace X]

theorem exists_measurePreserving_of_isProperMap {T : X → X} (hT : IsProperMap T) :
    ∃ μ : Measure X, μ.Regular ∧ MeasurePreserving T μ μ := by
  sorry

The proof uses a Banach limit φ . You can then construct a positive linear functional C_c(X, ℝ) →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ by the formula: Λ f = φ(f x, f (T x), f (T^[2] x), ...), which gives rise to a regular measure by RealRMK.rieszMeasure. This measure is invariant under T as Λ is invariant under T (by the definition of Banach limit). Properness (or compactness of fibers) is used to ensure that (a) f ∘ T is still in C_c(X, ℝ) for every f : C_c(X, ℝ) so that Λ (f ∘ T) is well-defined and (b) the pushforward of the riesz measure induced by Λ under the map T is still regular, so that we can use this uniqueness result MeasureTheory.Measure.ext_of_integral_eq_on_compactlySupported.

And of course when X is compact, properness is redundant. The only annoying part of this proof is that we don't have Banach limit in Mathlib right now.

I am not sure what it looks like if we want a local version (a version for an invariant set) of this result.

@Sébastien Gouëzel to clarify, do you want an invariant measure defined on the invariant set, or an invariant measure defined on the ambient space but supported on the invariant set? If the latter, the map needs to be at least measurable on the ambient space even if only the restriction to the invariant set is continuous

I want the invariant measure to be defined on the ambient space, and supported on the invariant set. There should be no measurability requirement on the whole space once we fix MeasurePreserving to only require ae-measurability instead of measurability as it is now.
Okay, that makes sense! And, since I'm still new to this, would that change to MeasurePreserving typically be in this PR or its own? Or is that change already in progress?
@Yongxi Lin (Aaron) That's a nice generalisation. I would be inclined to leave this as a TODO in the KB module, especially since Banach limits would need to be added

Yongxi Lin (Aaron) said:

I have also thought about this but I was not able to have time to implement this, and I claim that we can prove the following more general version:

This version is trivial, just take for mu the zero measure. The point of Krylov-Bogoliubov is that it gives you a probability measure, and this is not possible in general for a proper map on a locally compact space (think of a translation on the real line).
That's fair, but at least this version does not assume HasOuterApproxClosed, where the proof in #42947 relies on it.
And when the space is compact, Λ 1 = 1 which explains why the induced measure is a probability measure, and also this version further claims that the induced probability measure is regular.

Are you sure you don't need HasOuterApproxClosed? You get a functional on compactly supported continuous functions, which is invariant, and to which you can associate a measure by Riesz theorem. The preimage under f of this measure integrates compactly supported continuous functions in the same way, but this doesn't tell you that this is the same measure -- unless there are enough continuous functions to approximate all measurable sets, and this is exactly what HasOuterApproxClosed gives you.

Jeremy Parker said:

Since I'm still new to this, would that change to MeasurePreserving typically be in this PR or its own? Or is that change already in progress?

That change has been discussed and there is maybe already progress on it, so I'd say don't think about it. Just do your PR assuming that the map is globally measurable, and we'll change that after the refactor.

Let μ be the probability measure induced by Λ when the underlying space X is compact and Hausdorff. I believe you are asking whether Measure.map T μ is equal to μ. To prove this, you need to use MeasureTheory.Measure.ext_of_integral_eq_on_compactlySupported and show that Measure.map T μ is regular. As μ is regular, it is also InnerRegularCompactLTTop by MeasureTheory.Measure.Regular.instInnerRegularCompactLTTop, and then you can apply MeasureTheory.Measure.InnerRegularWRT.map to deduce that Measure.map T μ is InnerRegularCompactLTTop. You can then apply MeasureTheory.Measure.InnerRegularCompactLTTop.instRegularOfBorelSpaceOfR1SpaceOfIsFiniteMeasure to deduce that Measure.map T μ is regular.

I don't think HasOuterApproxClosed is used anywhere in my proof.
You're right!

@Sébastien Gouëzel when you say you want the version for an invariant set, I guess you just mean forward invariant? Either way, the current definitions in Dynamics.Flow are a bit clunky to use for a map. There is also #41940 open, tangentially related

@Jeremy Parker I'd prefer to see the proof I suggested implemented here. It's considerably harder, but it's more general and gives a stronger result. Otherwise I'm likely to open a PR later replacing this argument of averaging over delta measures — so it may save duplicated effort to go with the general version now.

@Yongxi Lin (Aaron) I believe I can remove HasOuterApproxClosed from the final statement but broadly keep my method of proof (which is more or less the standard route for KB) without needing to introduce Banach limits. I'll have a go tomorrow

I am not convinced the Banach limit gives anything more general. The key in Jeremy's approach is to use the compactness of the space of probability measures, which is proved using Riesz representation theorem and ultrafilters, so the same tools as in your argument. See the proof of docs#isCompact_setOfPred_finiteMeasure_le_of_compactSpace. This proof gives limit points which are regular measures (because they're constructed using Riesz!), so Jeremy's proof also gives a regular measure, although this is not obvious from current API.

I think I am just trying to say that this theorem should hold in a compact hausdorff space and the measure is regular. I am happy to see a proof that bypasses the argument of banach limit as long as it proves the general version I suggested.
(docs#MeasureTheory.Measure.exists_regular_eq_of_compactSpace could also be useful to get the regularity for free)

Jeremy Parker said:

Sébastien Gouëzel when you say you want the version for an invariant set, I guess you just mean forward invariant?

Yes, forward invariant, i.e., MapsTo f K K.

#42947 updated: it no longer requires HasOuterApproxClosed and there is a second theorem, for forward invariant compact sets. Personally, I would prefer an actual mathlib definition for forward invariant, but for now MapsTo is okay
The results now also state that the measure is regular

I am also interested in this result, thanks for PRing it! I would make another review about how the lemmas can be simplified by using the birkhoffAverage API, but it required some auxiliary lemmas, so I made my review into a commit here: link.

For it to pass CI you should also merge master, but I am not doing that in the PR to avoid polluting the diff.
